KAP Graduates 20 Beninese Filmmakers, Two Films Set for AFRIFF
Twenty young Beninese filmmakers have graduated from the KAP-SOPA Pan-African Filmmaking Bootcamp, with two of the three short films produced during the programme set to screen at the next edition of the Africa International Film Festival (AFRIFF).
The opportunity was announced by AFRIFF founder and Executive Director, Chioma Ude, during the graduation and premiere of the films at KAP Film Village and Resort in Igbojaye, Oyo State.
Ude announced that two of the films would be screened in the Students’ Film category at the next edition of AFRIFF, giving the graduates an opportunity to take their work beyond the training programme and into the wider festival circuit.
The 12-week programme was organised by KAP Film and Television Academy in partnership with the Government of the Republic of Benin through its audiovisual agency, SOPA. The participants began their training in Cotonou before continuing with practical training and production in Nigeria, where they completed the three short films.
The graduation brought together government and diplomatic representatives, filmmakers, producers, curators, educators and other figures from the African film industry.
Among those present were film curator Keith Shiri, Cameroonian filmmaker and educator Jean-Pierre Bekolo, filmmakers Tunde Kelani and Tade Ogidan, filmmaker and media executive Femi Odugbemi, international producer Virginie Besson-Silla, Ude and actress Sola Sobowale.
The structure of the KAP-SOPA programme combined filmmaking theory with practical production, mentorship and exposure to professional filmmaking environments. The participants moved from classroom instruction in Benin to hands-on production at KAP Film Village in Oyo State, allowing the students to complete original productions in a professional environment.
The graduation further saw the unveiling of ITAN, The Screen Gathering and Awards, a new platform championed by KAP Group founder Kunle Afolayan. Femi Odugbemi performed the unveiling.
ITAN is conceived as a platform to bring together filmmakers, producers, distributors, investors, policymakers, academics and other stakeholders involved in African cinema.

title: From campus mud to NYSC khaki: The inspiring story of Bitrus Nwalsu
content:
Bitrus Nwalsu
By CHRISTOPHER AMEH, Bauchi
Thirty-year-old Bitrus Nwalsu was recently spotted manoeuvring a locally-fabricated wheelchair through the heavy traffic of the busy Shafa Roundabout. He struggled cautiously to cross, a daily battle made necessary by the complete absence of accessible pedestrian infrastructure.
Read Also: Toyin Abraham rejects inclusion in Lagos APC campaign council
Nwalsu graduated in 2024 from the Abubakar Tatari Ali Polytechnic (ATAP), Bauchi, where he studied Business Administration. An indigene of Bauchi State, he hails from the Bogoro Local Government Area.
Nwalsu spoke passionately about his determination to pursue an education despite his physical disabilities and the constant discouragement from those around him.
“It wasn’t an easy journey, but I strongly believe that with God by my side, I will push through,” Nwalsu said. “Initially, securing admission was a major hurdle. But after all was said and done, I got in, struggled through, and graduated.”
Prior to entering the tertiary institution, Nwalsu had vowed that if he could make himself useful and secure a role as a civil servant, he would serve as a catalyst to lift up his family, his community, and others struggling around him.
“When I was growing up, I dreamed of becoming a good citizen of my country,” he shared. “I always wanted to be a pillar that would raise my family and the people around me. I constantly pray to God to make me a civil servant so I can take care of myself and those who are desperately in need.”
However, the road through ATAP Bauchi was paved with humiliation and frustration. Nwalsu recounted how some students refused to take him seriously or listen to his grievances simply because of his condition. While it initially demoralised him, he chose to encourage himself, holding onto the belief that he would one day be valuable to society.
Beyond the emotional toll and financial strains, the physical environment presented a constant barrier. His locally made wheelchair frequently broke down, particularly during the rainy season.
“It was a tough and painful experience during my school years,” Nwalsu recalled. “In many cases, I was ignored by my classmates because of my disability. People tended to dismiss me.
“On several occasions, I struggled just to get inside the lecture halls. Depending on where the class was allocated, I had to fight to get to the front just to hear the lecturer. During the rainy season, navigating the bad roads in my wheelchair was a nightmare. It would break down and constantly need repairs. It was truly an exhausting experience.”
Following his graduation, Nwalsu’s mobilisation for the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) came as a shock to many, especially his friends. People wondered how a physically challenged man could successfully navigate higher education and graduate.
Seeing him in the iconic NYSC uniform drew significant attention. Onlookers were flabbergasted to see him dressed in full NYSC attire while operating his manual wheelchair. Unable to believe their eyes, some onlookers even asked if someone had simply given him the uniform as a gift.
Conversely, many others commended him for passing through the four walls of a tertiary institution and emerging victorious. They hailed him as a shining example of how determination pays off.
“I feel encouraged and happy whenever I see people celebrating my success. Their commendation makes me stronger,” he said.
NYSC camp experience
Nwalsu shared with Vanguard how he was treated when he initially reported to the NYSC Orientation Camp in Jigawa State. Due to his physical condition, camp officials exempted him from the rigorous camp drills and redeployed him to his state of origin — a decision that brought him immense relief.
“I was terrified at first when I saw my posting, wondering how I would cope with the physical training,” he admitted. “Thank God they considered my condition and redeployed me back to Bauchi. I was so excited.”
Reflecting on the root cause of his predicament, Nwalsu explained that he became disabled at the age of two. He was born healthy with both legs, but a lack of early polio immunisation led to his permanent disability, exacerbated by inadequate medical treatments at the time.
He admitted that he initially felt deep anger when his parents explained the delayed treatment that altered his life, but he eventually came to terms with the reality that proper healthcare was scarce in his community back then.
“I was born with two functional legs,” he explained. “My parents told me they were unable to get me the early polio vaccine, which resulted in my condition. It wasn’t easy to accept. I was very unhappy when I grew up and discovered the cause, but I had to encourage myself and keep pushing through life.”
Nwalsu’s educational hurdles began long before college. Throughout primary and secondary school, his daily commute was his greatest impediment. Lacking a wheelchair at the time, he had to crawl long distances on the ground just to acquire his First School Leaving Certificate and complete his secondary education.
“My primary and secondary school days were not fun at all,” Nwalsu said.
“I didn’t have a wheelchair back then, so I literally crawled on the earth to get to school. Sometimes, due to our poor financial status, there was no food to eat. I was only able to push through to the end of my secondary education because of the constant encouragement from my mother.”
Social isolation also plagued his youth. From childhood, making friends was a struggle, as his peers routinely neglected him. Even today, he lacks close friends, noting that most people are ashamed to associate with him due to his physical state.
Despite these hardships, Nwalsu found joy outside academics. He got married in 2024—the same year he graduated — and has since been blessed with a beautiful baby girl. However, courting was filled with rejection, as multiple women turned him down because of his disability.
“When I felt it was time to settle down, I approached a girl I loved and had been courting. But she rejected my proposal when I told her I wanted to marry her. I am certain it was because of how I look,” he shared. “Eventually, I met another woman who loved me exactly as I am. When I proposed, she agreed, and we went through the marriage rites. Today, we are husband and wife.”
Because his wife is able-bodied, she took eight months to deeply ponder his proposal before ultimately accepting.
The marriage plans also sparked anxiety within his own family. His parents initially refused to believe he was ready, pointing out that he had just graduated, had no steady business, and did not farm. Fearing how the young couple would survive, his parents were deeply uncomfortable.
“My parents were worried about how we would feed,” Nwalsu recalled. “All I could tell them was that God would provide. After everything was said and done, they finally gave us their blessing.”
Today, Nwalsu is serving his fatherland at the Federal Secretariat in Bauchi. Yet, even as a youth corps member, accessibility remains his greatest barrier. Climbing the steep staircases of the secretariat just to complete his monthly clearance is a painful, exhausting chore.
Nwalsu closed his narrative with an emotional plea, calling on the Federal Government of Nigeria to prioritise accessibility laws and create a more inclusive society for people living with disabilities.

title: Itogon Mountain Village builds a home for love above the clouds
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Itogon Mountain Village in Benguet has transformed from a small family café into a popular mountain destination featuring cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel, all designed to showcase the stunning Cordillera landscape.
- The Bernabe family, who initially opened Café Stella, expanded their business in response to customer demand for private events, leading to the creation of additional facilities while preserving the natural environment.
- The venue emphasizes inclusivity and local culture, hosting various celebrations and working with local suppliers, while promoting environmental sustainability and heritage preservation in the rugged mountainous region.
ITOGON, Benguet – You notice the mountains before almost anything else.
They appear through the glass walls, between the pines beside the cabins, and behind the altar of a wooden chapel where nearly every direction opens to another ridge.
At Itogon Mountain Village, the view is not decoration. It is the point.
The three-hectare property in Barangay Loacan has grown from a small family café into a mountain destination with cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel designed around an almost 360-degree view of the Cordillera landscape.
On September 19, after weeks of habagat rain, the sun finally returned. The timing coincided with the property’s first wedding open house, Love Above the Clouds, but the experience made clear why people had begun coming here long before the flowers, gowns, and reception tables arrived.
The Bernabe family made a simple bet: that people would leave the city for the mountains, and that the mountains themselves were enough.
It started with coffee
Itogon Mountain Village did not begin with plans for weddings. It began with Café Stella.
“We started off very small,” said lawyer Rish Bernabe, one of the family members behind the property.
There were about six employees and only around 15 items on the menu, she recalled. Their father had envisioned a café down the mountain, while the family, which had long spent holidays in Baguio and the surrounding highlands, took on the challenge of running it.
Opening outside Baguio was a gamble. The place is almost half an hour away from the city, so “building up a business here was really a risk,” Rish said. Then people came.
The café gained attention on social media, and a kitchen designed for a modest number of customers suddenly had to feed far more. So they expanded the kitchen, upgraded to commercial equipment, hired more workers, and opened more of the building.
From a handful of employees, the enterprise eventually grew to around 80, according to the family.
Customers then began asking to reserve the café for private events. Closing the restaurant for an entire celebration was difficult, so the family expanded again.
Cabins followed. Then the Chapel of the Mountains. Then Montesierra, a dedicated events space.
What started as somewhere to eat had become somewhere people wanted to stay, gather, and mark important days.
Building around the mountain
The growth could easily have changed what drew people there. But the Bernabes say they tried not to let that happen.
Glass dominates much of the architecture so that the surrounding mountains remain visible. Buildings and roads were adjusted around existing trees whenever possible, they said.
One tree remains standing in the middle of a road because the family refused to cut it.
“This is the yamang lupa that made us come here,” Rish said. “So we really have to preserve it and celebrate it.”
That approach is most evident at the Chapel of the Mountains.
Wooden pews face an altar framed by glass, pines, and distant slopes. Light falls through the roof. Turn to either side, and the landscape remains part of the room.
On that sunny September afternoon, after a long stretch of rain, no manufactured backdrop could really compete.
The chapel is also deliberately non-sectarian. It is not accredited by the Roman Catholic Church to host Catholic sacramental weddings, management clarified after earlier confusion over a ceremony held there.
Rish said the couple involved had already been legally married in Manila and that the ceremony at the chapel was symbolic.
“We respect the rules of the diocese,” she said.
The space remains open to other ceremonies consistent with legal and religious requirements.
Its openness, then, is not only architectural. It gives couples and families from different traditions a place to celebrate in their own way.
Love beyond weddings
That idea of inclusion was central to the September 19 gathering.
“Today is about love, and not just romantic love,” said Suzy Mejia Bernabe, who handles marketing and sales for the family enterprise.
She spoke about weddings, birthdays, anniversaries, reunions, and other milestones, but also about creating a place where people could “slow down and reconnect.”
The family says it works with local suppliers, uses local produce when possible, and invites local makers, artists, and cultural performers to take part in events. That puts the property within a broader effort by Itogon to build tourism around its landscape and culture.
The municipality has long been associated with gold. Its own historical account traces gold working in the area to Indigenous communities before the colonial period, while large-scale mining later shaped much of the town’s modern history.
Today, Itogon’s tourism program also promotes nature and culture, with environmental sustainability, heritage preservation, and local employment among its stated goals.
The setting comes with limits. Itogon is rugged mountain country, with 74.6% of its land classified as having slopes steeper than 50%, according to the municipal government.
The Bernabes know building here is different from building on flatter ground. The terrain dictates what can be done, where structures can go, and sometimes which trees have to stay exactly where they are.
Perhaps that is why the place works. It does not feel as though the mountain was flattened to make room for a destination. In places, the destination appears to have negotiated with the mountain.
Looking up
For generations, Itogon has been known for what lies beneath its mountains: gold.
Itogon Mountain Village asks visitors to look up instead. At the pines growing beside the buildings. At the ridges beyond the glass. At a chapel where mountains remain visible behind the altar.
The family started with a small café and the uncertainty that anyone would drive this far from the city. But now, people come not only for coffee, but to stay, celebrate, marry, or simply spend a few hours where the mountains are allowed to remain the biggest thing in the room.
Perhaps the distance is not something visitors have to overcome after all. Perhaps it is part of the point. – Rappler.com

title: Apple store sued after using disabled bathroom as storage, change room
content:
Apple has been ordered to pay damages to a former employee at its Canberra Centre store whose disability requires frequent and sudden use of a bathroom.
The man often had to wait to use standard toilets because the accessible toilet was used for storage, as a change room, and to access a cleaner's closet.
What's next?
The ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal dismissed the man's complaints of direct discrimination, but awarded him $18,000 for indirect discrimination.
Tech giant Apple has been ordered to pay a former employee of its Canberra store $18,000 in compensation for indirect discrimination over access to the shop's toilets.
The man, who worked at the store in the Canberra Centre from late 2019 to early 2024, had a bowel condition requiring frequent and sudden use of a bathroom.
Until renovations were completed in 2024, the store's accessible bathroom was used variously for storage, as a change room, and to access a cleaner's closet.
It meant the man often had to wait to use the store's standard staff toilets, and when he did use the accessible bathroom, the stored equipment made it "very tight and unsafe".
He made a complaint to the ACT Human Rights Commission, who referred the case to the territory's Civil and Administrative Tribunal.
The man sought $20,000 for past economic loss, and $50,000 in general compensation.
Apple argued the equipment had been stored in the accessible toilet due to a lack of space elsewhere in the store, and managers had been flexible in allowing the man to take breaks where needed and use the shopping centre's public toilets.
Discrimination not 'intentional, calculated or cruel'
In a decision published this month, senior tribunal member Robert Orr found the man hadn't been directly discriminated against.
But he found the man had been disadvantaged because of his disability, and the onus had been on Apple to demonstrate the arrangements in the store were reasonable.
"This was not a case where the discrimination made out was intentional, calculated or cruel," Mr Orr said.
"Rather, this was a case of indirect discrimination where [Apple] put in place quickly those measures it could to address the applicant's bathroom complaints, and in time addressed all his complaints, and generally sought to assist the applicant to manage his condition.
"In my view there was a condition or requirement that the applicant use the standard bathroom.
"This had the effect of disadvantaging the [man] because of his disability which required him to go to the toilet often and suddenly.
"The fact that notwithstanding these factors he could manage to use the accessible toilet, or another toilet, does not defeat the claim."
The tribunal ruled no medical evidence had been provided for the man's claim of psychological injury, nor had there been appropriate evidence for his loss of earnings.
"These features mean that a significant amount of compensation cannot be ordered," Mr Orr said.
The tribunal dismissed the man's claims over his rejected work from home requests, finding no basis it was due to his disability.
But it ordered Apple to pay the man $18,000 in compensation for the indirect discrimination complaint.

title: Após mobilização da comunidade, prefeitura de Araucária envia máquinas para desobstrução de áreas alagadas
content:
Nessa quarta-feira (16), a comunidade Rio Negro e o Movimento Popular por Moradia (MPM) estiveram em uma reunião com representantes da Secretaria Municipal de Obras Públicas e Transportes de Araucária (PR), após enchentes atingirem 35 famílias da ocupação. No mesmo dia, a prefeitura do município enviou retroescavadeiras para retirar terra e entulhos que obstruíam vias e cursos d’água.

As lideranças reivindicaram investimentos na infraestrutura do território com limpeza, drenagem e manutenção dos cursos d’água. Além disso, cobraram a necessidade de um plano de emergência com apoio e subsídios às famílias atingidas.
Sobre as ações comunitárias para pressionar ações do poder público na região, o MPM afirmou em nota, no Instagram: “Organização popular para conquistar respostas imediatas e soluções permanentes!”

title: Earn nothing? Pay nothing: 81-year-old Ahmedabad doctor charges patients based on their monthly income
content:
What if the amount you pay for a doctor’s consultation depended on how much you earn?
An 81-year-old ENT surgeon in Ahmedabad, Dr Nandlal Manseta, follows an unconventional fee system that allows patients to pay based on their income. Those with no income can consult him for free.
At his clinic, Manseta follows a simple sliding-scale model. Patients are not asked to submit income certificates or any other documents. Instead, the fee is decided on the basis of what they earn, with patients depositing the amount in a small donation box at the clinic.
According to the fee chart displayed at the clinic, someone earning Rs 1,000 pays Rs 10 for a consultation, while a monthly income of Rs 10,000 corresponds to a Rs 100 fee. Those earning Rs 1 lakh pay Rs 1,000. For patients with no income, the consultation is free.
Manseta follows this practice as part of his effort to give back to society. His approach is rooted in the belief that a person’s financial situation should not prevent them from seeking medical care.
View this post on Instagram
The doctor has also spoken about how support from society and the government played an important role in his own journey. He now tries to pay it forward.
The Better India recently shared Manseta’s story on social media. An overlay on the post featured one of his quotes: “If a patient’s income is zero, the fee is zero too.”
The story has since sparked a strong response online, with several users praising the doctor for making consultations more accessible.
“What a relief to patients who can’t afford to pay, but have Doctors like him who believe in treating patients. God bless him,” one user wrote.
“The ones with max income act the most privilidged don’t pay and create more fuss also,” another commented.
“Best thing is written below ‘no income proof needed’. Honesty is contagious,” a third user said.
“Even thousands of patients surgery were funded by manseta sir foundation,” another person shared.

title: Boulgou/Zabré : La commune récompense les meilleurs élèves et enseignants

Boulgou/Zabré : La commune récompense les meilleurs élèves et enseignants
Zabré, 18 sept. 2026 (AIB)-La commune de Zabré a célébré, vendredi 18 septembre 2026 à la Place de la Nation, l’excellence scolaire au titre des années 2025 et 2026, en récompensant les meilleurs élèves, enseignants et encadreurs.
Au total, 4 motos, 7 ordinateurs, 2 tablettes, 15 vélos, 60 kits scolaires et des attestations de reconnaissance ont été décernés aux différents lauréats.
Pour la CEB de Zabré 1, Gouba Julienne a été distinguée meilleure élève en 2025 avec une moyenne de 8,94/10, tandis que Gambo Oussounssoum Arielle a obtenu le titre en 2026 avec 9,61/10.
Dans la CEB de Zabré 2, Nanga Wendtouma Patricia, a été la meilleure élève au CEP 2025 avec une moyenne de 8,88/10. En 2026, cette distinction est revenue à Seihon Hamida, avec 9,36/10.
Chez les enseignants, Koampaba Couldiati , de l’école de Bango, a été distingué meilleur enseignant de la CEB de Zabré 1 en 2025, avec 66 élèves présentés au CEP et tous admis. En 2026, Fati Guengani/Yabré , de Zabré-Filles A, a enregistré un taux de réussite de 100 % avec 62 élèves.
Pour la CEB de Zabré 2, Moctar Tarnagda de l’école Zabré B, a été désigné meilleur enseignant en 2025, après avoir présenté 59 élèves, tous admis, soit un taux de réussite de 100 %. En 2026, Aline Ouangrawa K. également de l’école Zabré B a obtenu la distinction de meilleure enseignante avec 71 élèves présentés et 71 admis, soit également 100 % de réussite.
Pour cette sixième édition, l’excellence scolaire a été célébrée sous le thème : « Excellence à l’école primaire et secondaire, un engagement pour la résilience et le patriotisme ».
L’innovation majeure de cette édition a été la reconnaissance du mérite des meilleurs bacheliers des séries A et D, récompensés avec des tablettes, des meilleurs brevetés, qui ont reçu des vélos, et du meilleur enseignant du secondaire, récompensé avec un ordinateur portable.
Dans son mot de bienvenue, le Camarade PDS de Zabré, Alain Boubié Bassono, a félicité les lauréats et remercié les partenaires ayant contribué à la réussite de l’activité. Il a notamment souligné qu’« aucune récompense en elle-même ne suffit pour épuiser la reconnaissance de toute la communauté à l’endroit de l’enseignement ».
Le Camarade PDS de Bagré, W. Gérard Maré, représentant le président de la cérémonie, le Camarade Haut-Commissaire de la province du Boulgou, a transmis les félicitations de ce dernier aux organisateurs et aux lauréats. Le Haut-Commissaire, qui souhaitait être présent, a été empêché par une cérémonie du même genre à Tenkodogo, a-t-il expliqué. Selon le représentant du Camarade Haut-Commissaire, la « Craie d’or » constitue un moment de reconnaissance du travail, de la discipline, de la persévérance et du mérite. Il a invité les lauréats à redoubler d’efforts.
Émue par cette reconnaissance, la lauréate Guengani/Yabré Fati a estimé que cette distinction l’interpelle à redoubler d’efforts. « Le seul secret de la réussite pour moi est le don de soi et la passion du travail. Je dédie la moto que j’ai eue à mes responsables et surtout à mes collègues et à ma famille », a-t-elle déclaré.
Initiée par arrêté en 2019, la célébration de l’excellence scolaire vise à reconnaître le mérite des meilleurs élèves et enseignants de la commune de Zabré.

title: Getting away from gunshots
content:
It has been over a week since Jish (name changed to protect privacy) arrived in India after completing his mandatory military service in Israel. He savours a lemon pie and ginger tea at a popular vegan bakery-cum-café located in the narrow market lane of Dharamkot, a misty village in Himachal Pradesh’s rain-washed pine forests. A popular destination among Israeli backpackers along the Hummus Trail, Dharamkot is about two-three kilometres uphill from Mcleodganj. “This is my second visit to India,” he says, just before setting off for his painting class — one of the ways he chooses to unwind in the Himalayan landscape.
He felt compelled to visit last year in May, hearing stories through the drumbeat of social media and his friends’ first-hand accounts. He stayed in the country for nearly five months, first alone, and then for two and half months with his wife. “I travelled mostly in the Himalayas on a motorcycle. I came to Dharamkot, then went to Manali’s Parvati Valley, and then to Ladakh. On my second visit to India, we [my wife and I] have come together,” says Jish, who has served his conscription term of two years in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF)’s reserve military service.
Even as the former soldier made plans to travel, the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran left its mark on his life. “Since October 2023, we have lost many friends and many civilians. It’s like an endless war between two nations, the Jewish nation and the Arab nation. Just one month before Hamas attacked us in October 2023, I got engaged. I was on the battlefield. My fiancé prepared all the stuff, you know, the wedding dress, and so on. It’s difficult,” says 25-year-old Jish, who says he joined the IDF when he was 19.
Dharamkot is known as Mini Israel, because a number of Israelis flock here after they complete their conscription terms. Around 80,000 Israelis visit India annually, according to a paper, ‘Decoding the hummus trail of India: regaining the lost prudence’, published in 2022 in Anatolia, an international journal of tourism and hospitality research. “Last year, a little over 1 lakh foreign tourists visited Himachal. This included visitors from Europe, Canada, the U.S., and Israel among other countries,” says Bhanu Gupta, joint director at Himachal’s Tourism department.
This year, however, Dharamkot’s narrow, stone-paved roads lined by tall pine trees look relatively deserted. The influx of Israeli travellers has been skewed and uneven, according to local hospitality players. Yet, over the years, the steady footfall of foreign tourists has helped the economy of this tiny village, even as the locals worry about the adverse impact of drug-laced raves in the forest.
Trailing peace
Jish says he and his wife are “here to relax” and will soon head out on their hired bike to Delhi and onward to Rajasthan. In Dharamkot, “There are different courses, like music sessions, yoga, drawing, and painting — there are so many options to unwind. In India, unlike Israel, there is more peace and Nature, landscapes, and special people,” he says, as he grabs his belongings to move for his painting class in lower Dharamkot, run by residents largely through hired instructors. Charcoal painting and pencil sketching are popular among foreign tourists in this Himalayan village.
For Jish, the trip to India is more than just about travelling. “There is a strong and deep connection between Israel and India, like a religious connection and some shared values between these two nations. India is different from Western societies that are materialistic. The trust factor is what’s really attractive in India,” says Jish, who will soon start a course in Judaism philosophy in Israel this October. He will be in India until then.
The Hummus Trail gets its name from hummus — a Middle Eastern food traditionally made from cooked chickpeas, tahini (sesame paste), lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil. The trail has many cafés and restaurants catering to Israeli travellers. The route spans several places in the mighty mountains of the Himalayas, like Kasol, Old Manali, Rishikesh, and Ladakh. It stretches across Uttar Pradesh’s Varanasi and Pushkar in Rajasthan, extending to South Goa, Gokarna and Hampi in Karnataka, and Vattakanal in Tamil Nadu.
Hodaya, 23, also from Israel, has come to Dharamkot with her friend, drawn by the popularity of the Hummus Trail. “Most Israelis follow the Shvil Hummus (Hummus Trail) route in India and Nepal, as it has many cafés with Hebrew menus, Israeli music, and food. I have been in India for about two months now, travelling between Manali, Leh, and Dharamkot. It’s relaxing here,” says Hodaya, who is set to return to Israel in a couple of days. Asked how she feels about the ongoing conflict, she shrugs it off with a smile, saying, “I am used to it, so I am not stressed anymore.”
Monetising Israeli tourism
The stone walls across Dharamkot are dotted with posters in Hebrew, alongside English. In lower Dharamkot, more accessible by road than the upper areas, the bulletin boards outside cafés, restaurants, roadside stalls, and homestays on the market stretch, serve as a news feed for different events for the village’s international community. There are wellness workshops, music and art events, community activities, and notices for parties.
Narender Pathania, 54, who runs an eight-room guest house in Dharamkot, points out that the flow of Israeli travellers has been unsteady for the past three years. The first lull, he says, was in 2023. That year, on October 7, Hamas-led Palestinian armed groups crossed into southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people.
Soon, the century-old Israel-Palestine conflict — one of the longest and most-violent in the world — escalated, as Israel intensified attacks on Palestine. At least 20,179 children were killed and 44,143 children injured as a direct result of attacks on Gaza between October 7, 2023, and October 7, 2025, according to a UN commission report released on June 23, 2026. “The current total is certainly higher. Thousands of children are feared to be buried under rubble. In the 300 days after the ceasefire was announced 300 more children were killed — one child every day with still hundreds more, injured,” according to UNICEF.
The tourists, Pathania says, further dropped after the US-Israel and Iran conflict broke out in February 2026. “Almost all of them had left when the war with Iran started. Now some have returned, but the flow is lower. All my rooms, which used to be packed during these days, are vacant. It eventually brings loss. Tourism is the primary livelihood for many in our village,” he says.
Pathania adds that Israelis’ Indian sojourn lasts several months, so they prefer budget-friendly homestays over expensive hotels. “Of late, tourists come with their children. Many cafés here cater specifically to the food preferences of Israelis. They visit Manali, Srinagar, Ladakh, and even trek to Chamba from here. They go to meditation centres, lean towards spirituality. Many lie in the lush green field for hours, just relaxing,” he adds.
Vivek Kumar hails from neighbouring Dharamshala, manages routine affairs at ’Dharamkot studio’ that offers pottery and ceramic courses in Dharamkot. He says, “Among the foreigners who come to us, Israelis make up the largest share. We have different courses ranging from five to 35 days. A minimum two-hour workshop is also available to experience the process of shaping wet clay into finished objects. Most of those who enrol with us are Israelis. In their country, these things are quite expensive, as I understand from speaking with them,” he says.
Sanjeev Gandhi, chief advisor to the Hotel and Restaurant Association, Smart City, Dharamshala, who himself runs Hotel Gandhi’s Paradise at Dharamkot, shares his experience on why Israelis are drawn to the town: “Most Israelis come carrying the weight of war and stress. They come to forget. What they value most about Dharamshala is the silence,” says Gandhi, recalling a number of them telling him that the biggest draw is that they don’t hear gunshots.
Not all Israelis need to serve conscription though. There are military exemptions for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish community, who constitute about 13% of the population. This has triggered protests in the past, also leading to some stress among communities.
Rage against the rave
The Hummus Trail, also notorious as the Hashish Trail, is a route taken for readily available cheap drugs, says the Anatolia paper. In June 2026, taking suo motu action, the Himachal Pradesh High Court directed the transfer of three senior officers, including the then Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police of Kullu district, in connection with the alleged nexus between officials and organisers of big-scale rave parties in Kullu district.
The drug issue was addressed in the 2007 Israeli-Canadian documentary Flipping Out, directed by Yoav Shamir. It follows Israeli soldiers after their discharge as they travel to India, exploring drug use and the psychological breakdowns some experience. The film also documents Israeli officials’ response, including a meeting between the then Deputy Prime Minister Eli Yishai and former soldiers.
Om Prakash Sharma, a former Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) officer, who handled several enforcement operations in Himachal, Punjab, and Jammu-Kashmir, while he worked with the NCB’s Chandigarh zone from 2002 to 2007, asserts that cultivation of cannabis and opium in remote areas of Kullu district and Mandi district of Himachal continues unabated.
“The narcotics trade cannot survive unless there’s support from the socio-political and administrative strata. Foreigners have been found involved in the illicit drug trade,” he says, adding that regular Himachali people get involved because of “local poverty” and “easy money”. The modus operandi is simple — they throw money at people. They know that forest lands and even private lands are available for cultivation at a meagre sum, he says. “These people, usually with Nepalese and other labourers, then cultivate and harvest it, after which the networks of foreigners operate its trade. Foreigners have even been marrying local women as a part of their strategy as well.”
During his tenure, Sharma busted many drug deals, including 155 kilograms of charas (hashish) in Chandigarh, smuggled out of Kullu by Israeli, Czech Republic, and Indian (Kullu) nationals, and bound for Amsterdam in 2005. “During our operations, we had recovered the foreign strain of the cannabis seeds from some foreigners’ houses. That was a hybrid seed, which clearly points to the extent of foreign involvement in the illicit drug trade,” says Sharma, who has also served as convener-cum-advisor of the Himachal Pradesh Nasha Nivaran Board, formed to curb the drug menace.
“Rave parties in secluded forest areas are being organised in the name of tourism, which is not possible without the shelter of bigwigs and administrative machinery and local political patronage,” he adds.
Monika Pathania, former councillor of Dharamkot ward, which falls under Dharamshala Municipal Corporation, says, “People talk about rave parties happening here, but that’s simply not true. Such things don’t happen at all in the village. It could be happening in remote areas where police presence is minimal, but in Dharamkot and neighbouring Bhagsunag there are police check posts to keep a tab on unlawful activities.” She insists the village is only known for its meditation centres.
Ashwani Bamba, president of the Dharamsala Hotel and Restaurant Association, explains that Israelis tend to travel in groups and usually they prefer to spend less on accommodation, but are willing to indulge when it comes to food and, as he puts it, “Other things.” Recalling that things were different a decade or so ago, Bamba points out that then, drug consumption was open. Now, not so much.
Gandhi is worried that locals too are impacted by drugs. “We have been urging the locals and administration to create a joint team to tackle the drug menace,” he says.
For many young Israelis like Jish, Dharamkot is an escape from war, a holiday of healing and hash.
